summaries.example: Imagine looking at two drawings. You like one because its shapes and colors work well together. This is more than saying, “I enjoy it.” You may also think other people have good reasons to like it, even if they disagree. You can change your mind later, too, because your first judgment may have been mistaken.
summaries.summary: Aesthetic judgment is thinking about beauty, ugliness, elegance, or similar features. The entry focuses especially on judgments of taste, such as “This painting is beautiful.” These judgments begin with a personal feeling of pleasure or displeasure, so they are subjective. Yet they do not feel like ordinary choices, such as choosing a favorite snack. When we confidently call something beautiful, we usually act as if others should be able to agree and as if some judgments could be wrong. This makes aesthetic judgments both feeling-based and normative: they make a claim about what is fitting or correct. The difficult question is how a personal feeling can support a judgment that reaches beyond one person. Kant tried to answer this by saying that pleasure in beauty is not based on wanting to own or use the beautiful thing. He also connected beauty with the shared abilities of human thinking. The entry explains that this proposal is important but debated. It also distinguishes beauty from simple agreeableness, considers whether beauty depends on features of objects and their contexts, and asks whether there are general rules of taste. The entry presents the idea that beauty depends on non-aesthetic features without being produced by a simple formula. It ends by examining whether many aesthetic ideas, including elegance and sublimity, can belong to one organized group.
key_ideas: Aesthetic judgments are based on feelings, unlike ordinary judgments about measurable facts.
They are different from simple likes, because we often think other people ought to see the beauty too.
Thinking something is beautiful does not automatically make it beautiful.
Beauty depends on features of the thing, even though there may be no simple rule that always tells us what will be beautiful.
Kant called pleasure in beauty “disinterested,” meaning it is not just the pleasure of getting something we want.
Philosophers disagree about how beauty, pleasure, and correctness are connected.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps explain why people can disagree about art, music, nature, or everyday objects while still discussing their reasons seriously. It also shows why “Everyone has a different taste” may be too simple: some preferences are merely personal, but aesthetic judgments often aim at wider agreement. Thinking about beauty teaches us to separate feelings, facts, reasons, and judgments without pretending that every disagreement has an easy answer.

important_terms.definition: A judgment about beauty, ugliness, or another aesthetic feature. It comes from a feeling but also presents itself as more than a private preference.
A feeling of liking or disliking that helps support an aesthetic judgment.
The idea that some judgments about beauty are more fitting or correct than others.
The idea that beauty depends on features of a thing, such as its shape, colors, sounds, or arrangement, but does not simply depend on what one person thinks.

questions_to_think_about: Is saying “I like this song” different from saying “This song is beautiful”? How?
Can you think of something you once judged beautiful but now see differently?
Should a beautiful thing have certain features, or is beauty only in the viewer?
Can something be both beautiful and powerful or overwhelming?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says that a minimalist building is elegant because of its balanced proportions, limited materials, and carefully placed openings. Another student says it is cold and uninteresting. Their disagreement is not exactly like disagreeing over a private food preference, but neither is it settled by measuring one physical feature. Each is making an aesthetic judgment that responds to the building’s nonaesthetic features and implicitly claims that one interpretation is more appropriate. The students may revise their judgments as they notice more about the building or its context.
summaries.summary: The entry examines what happens when we call something beautiful, ugly, elegant, delicate, or sublime. Its starting point is Kant’s account of the judgment of taste. Such a judgment is subjective because it is based on pleasure or displeasure rather than on a purely empirical description. But it also has a normative aspiration: when we call something beautiful, we generally present our judgment as appropriate and expect that others should be able to recognize its force. This differs from a judgment of agreeableness, such as saying that a food tastes good to us, where variation in individual preference is normally accepted. The central philosophical problem is how a response that is subjective can support a judgment with a claim that extends beyond the individual. Kant explains this through a shared harmony of imagination and understanding, though the entry treats that deeper account as controversial. Other possibilities include sentimentalist accounts, which emphasize cultivated feeling, and realist accounts, which treat beauty as a genuine feature of the world. The entry also considers three related commitments: aesthetic judgments are not made true by anyone’s belief, aesthetic properties depend on nonaesthetic properties, and aesthetic properties may lack strict laws or predictable rules. This combination—dependence without lawlike predictability—is not considered contradictory. Finally, the entry asks how to define “the aesthetic” as a wider category. A hierarchical proposal makes beauty and ugliness central, treating properties such as elegance or delicacy as ways of being beautiful or ugly. key_ideas: Kant identifies subjectivity and a claim to universal validity as the two central features of judgments of taste.
Aesthetic judgments occupy a middle position: like preference judgments, they arise from responses; like empirical judgments, they aspire to correctness.
The normative force of aesthetic judgment may be grounded in the feeling itself, in shared cognitive capacities, or in real aesthetic properties; the entry does not treat one explanation as settled.
Beauty is mind-independent in the modest sense that believing something beautiful does not make it so, while beauty also depends on nonaesthetic features.
Dependence or supervenience need not amount to laws that predict aesthetic properties from physical or sensory descriptions.
Kant’s disinterestedness separates pleasure in beauty from desire, but whether beauty is wholly desire-free and whether only beauty produces such pleasure remain contested.
summaries.why_it_matters: Aesthetic judgment is a model case for studying how human thought can be both responsive and reason-guided. It raises questions about subjectivity, disagreement, expertise, realism, and the limits of rules. These questions matter whenever people evaluate art, architecture, music, nature, or design. The discussion also warns against two easy extremes: reducing aesthetics to whatever someone happens to like, or assuming that aesthetic correctness works exactly like scientific measurement.

important_terms.definition: A judgment grounded in pleasure or displeasure rather than simply in a report of an observable physical fact.
The feature of aesthetic judgment whereby it presents some responses or judgments as more appropriate, correct, or better than others.
Kant’s term for pleasure in beauty when that pleasure is not based on desire and does not, by itself, generate a desire for the object.
The claim that an object’s beauty does not become true merely because someone judges it beautiful.
The idea that aesthetic properties depend on nonaesthetic features, such as form, sound, appearance, arrangement, or context.
A relation in which aesthetic differences require corresponding differences in nonaesthetic features, without implying a simple predictive rule.
A broad proposed category in which judgments of beauty and ugliness are central, while properties such as elegance or delicacy may count as aesthetic through their relation to beauty.
The striking or overwhelming aesthetic quality associated by some theories with magnitude, power, danger, or extraordinary beauty; its relation to beauty is disputed.

questions_to_think_about: What kind of correctness could an aesthetic judgment have if it is based on a subjective response?
Does dependence on an object’s features support aesthetic realism, or can a non-realist theory explain it?
Why might there be aesthetic dependence without general laws of taste?
Is pleasure in beauty genuinely separate from wanting, acting, or personal history?
Should sublimity be treated as a kind of beauty, a different basic aesthetic category, or something that varies by case?

summaries.example: A class visits a sculpture in a park. Maya says it is graceful because its curved metal parts seem balanced and light. Jordan says it is awkward. They are not merely reporting their private moods: each seems to be giving a judgment that others could assess. Still, there is no simple measuring tool that settles the argument. If they learn that the sculpture was designed for a different space, or notice details they missed, their judgments might change.
summaries.summary: The entry asks what makes a judgment about beauty different from a simple statement of preference. A judgment of taste, such as “This song is beautiful,” has two important features. First, it is subjective: it rests on a feeling of pleasure or displeasure. Second, it is normative: it treats some responses as more appropriate or correct than others and seems to invite agreement from people generally. This puts taste judgments between two other kinds of judgment. They resemble personal preference because they arise from inner responses, but they resemble factual judgments because they aim at correctness. The tension between these features is the main philosophical problem. Kant argues that pleasure in beauty is disinterested, meaning it is not founded on desire for the object. He connects this pleasure with mental abilities that humans share. The entry explains why this might support a claim to universal validity, while also noting that Kant’s deeper explanation is controversial. It compares this approach with sentimentalist views that emphasize trained or cultivated feeling and realist views that regard beauty as a genuine property of things. The discussion then adds that beauty is not made true by an individual’s belief, but it does depend on non-aesthetic properties. For example, an artwork’s beauty may depend on its form, appearance, sounds, or context. That dependence does not guarantee a formula for predicting beauty; aesthetic judgment may remain “lawless” in the sense that no interesting general rule tells us exactly what aesthetic result follows from given features. The entry ends by examining the wider category of aesthetic judgment. One proposal makes judgments of beauty and ugliness central, with qualities such as elegance and delicacy understood as particular
key_ideas: Taste judgments come from feelings, but they usually present themselves as judgments that can be better or worse.
“Everyone has different tastes” fits ordinary preferences better than it fits confident judgments of beauty.
Beauty is not simply created by belief, yet it is connected to an object’s non-aesthetic features.
Aesthetic properties may depend on physical, sensory, or contextual features without following strict laws.
Kant’s idea of disinterested pleasure tries to explain how beauty can make a claim on everyone rather than only on people with a particular desire.
The category of the aesthetic may be organized around beauty and ugliness, but this proposal remains open to criticism.
summaries.why_it_matters: The philosophy of aesthetic judgment explains why conversations about art and beauty can involve genuine reasons without becoming scientific experiments. It gives us tools for distinguishing personal enjoyment from claims about what is beautiful, and for understanding why people may revise their judgments. It also shows that disagreement does not automatically prove that all judgments are equally good—or that one simple rule can settle every aesthetic question.

important_terms.definition: The feature of a taste judgment that it is based on a person’s feeling of pleasure or displeasure.
The idea that a taste judgment asks for more than personal agreement: it treats some responses as more fitting or correct.
Kant’s name for pleasure in beauty when it is not based on wanting to possess, use, or otherwise obtain the object.
The view that an object is not beautiful just because someone thinks it is beautiful.
The view that beauty depends on non-aesthetic features, such as an object’s shape, colors, sounds, arrangement, or setting.
A claim that aesthetic differences require differences in non-aesthetic features, even though no simple rule may predict the aesthetic result.
The proposed structure in which beauty and ugliness are basic, while features such as elegance or delicacy are aesthetic because they describe ways of being beautiful or ugly.
An aesthetic quality often connected with great size, power, or intensity. Philosophers disagree about whether it is opposed to beauty or is a special kind of beauty.

questions_to_think_about: Why do people criticize someone’s judgment of a song or painting but usually do not criticize a favorite flavor in the same way?
Can a person’s aesthetic judgment be wrong even if many people disagree with it?
What details of an artwork might its beauty depend on?
If there are no fixed rules of taste, how can criticism give reasons?
Does something frightening or enormous have to be beautiful in order to be sublime?
